Rounded answers inflate measured inequality

Abstract

People who report incomes and spending in surveys often round their answers. We show that rounding raises measured inequality by a few percent in ten national surveys and give a correction.

Similar content being viewed by others

  • Another article about surveys

Main

Survey answers cluster at multiples of ten and one hundred. When the true values are spread smoothly, this clustering adds spread at the top and bottom of the distribution, which makes inequality look larger than it is.

We estimate how much of each country's measured inequality comes from rounding alone, using the share of answers that end in zero.
